analogy.p: Imagine spraying a lawn with a weed killer that kills nearly every weed. A few weeds happen to have a natural resistance, so they survive, spread their seeds and soon the lawn is full of weeds the spray cannot kill. That is **antibiotic resistance**: the antibiotic is the selection pressure and the resistant bacteria are the survivors that reproduce. Stopping the spray part-way (not finishing the course) leaves the toughest weeds, and using the spray on plants it was not designed for (viruses) just wastes it and breeds tougher weeds. A **painkiller** is like painting over the bare patches so the lawn looks better, without killing the weeds at all. The analogy breaks down because weeds do not mutate in response to the spray; in bacteria, resistance genes arise by random mutation before treatment, and the antibiotic only selects them.

bullets: **Antibiotic** = a medicine (e.g. **penicillin**) that cures bacterial disease by killing bacteria (or stopping them reproducing) inside the body.
Antibiotics are **specific**: a given antibiotic works on certain bacteria, so the correct one must be chosen.
Antibiotics have **greatly reduced deaths** from infectious bacterial diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and infected wounds.
**Antibiotic-resistant strains** (for example **MRSA**) are a serious and growing concern.
**Antibiotics cannot kill viruses**, because viruses reproduce inside body cells and are not affected by drugs that target bacterial structures.
**Painkillers** treat **symptoms** (pain, fever) and **do not kill pathogens**.
Link: resistance is explained by **mutation and natural selection** (evolution topic) and testing antibiotics is the **required practical** with agar plates (Biology only, cell biology topic).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1.8 (Antibiotics and painkillers) states that **antibiotics such as penicillin are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body**. It is important that **specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics**. The use of antibiotics has **greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases**, but the **emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern**. **Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.** **Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill the pathogens.** Finally, it is **difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues**. These sentences are almost a mark scheme in themselves, so learn them as short facts and then learn the reasoning behind each.

bullets: **Penicillin** prevents the **bacterial cell wall** forming properly, so the bacterium bursts (lyses) because water enters by osmosis.
Human and animal cells have **no cell wall**, so penicillin does **not harm human cells**.
Other antibiotics target the bacterium's **ribosomes** (protein synthesis) or **DNA replication**; bacterial ribosomes differ from human ones.
The key idea is **selective toxicity**: it harms bacteria but not the host.
Some antibiotics are **narrow-spectrum** (work on a few types of bacteria) and others **broad-spectrum** (work on many types).
Antibiotics must reach the infection, so they are carried in the **blood**: taken by mouth, injected or applied locally.
Antibiotics do **not** work on **fungi, protists or viruses** because these are different kinds of cell or are not cells at all.
core.p: Antibiotics work because **bacterial cells are different from human cells**. Bacteria have a **cell wall** (made of a different material from the cellulose in plants), and they have their own enzymes and protein-making machinery. Many antibiotics attack structures or processes that **only bacteria have**, so they kill the bacteria but **do not harm the patient's own cells**. For example, **penicillin interferes with the building of the bacterial cell wall**, so the bacterium weakens and bursts as water enters by osmosis. Other antibiotics stop bacteria **making proteins** or **copying their DNA**. Some antibiotics **kill** bacteria (bactericidal) while others **stop them growing and dividing** (bacteriostatic), giving the immune system time to clear the infection.

bullets: **Specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics** (spec wording).
Doctors may take a **sample** (swab, urine, blood) and **grow a culture** to identify the bacteria and test which antibiotic works.
The **disc diffusion test** on agar shows which antibiotic has the biggest **zone of inhibition** (clear area).
Using a **narrow-spectrum** antibiotic where possible reduces the effect on useful **gut bacteria**.
Using the wrong antibiotic **delays treatment**, lets the infection spread and **increases resistance**.
Some infections are treated with more than one antibiotic at once (e.g. tuberculosis) to reduce the chance of resistance developing.
core.h: Why specific bacteria need specific antibiotics
core.p: Different bacteria have **different cell walls, enzymes and metabolic pathways**, so an antibiotic that damages one species may do nothing to another. For example, an antibiotic that works well on one kind of throat infection may be useless against a urinary tract infection caused by a different bacterium. For this reason doctors try to **identify the bacterium** causing the infection, often by **culturing a sample** and **testing it against several antibiotics** (as in the required practical). Using the **right antibiotic** for the right bacterium treats the patient most effectively and helps **reduce the spread of resistance**, because broad, unnecessary use puts more bacteria under selection pressure.

bullets: Fleming noticed that mould (*Penicillium*) on an agar plate **killed the bacteria around it**, which led to penicillin (history; useful context, not usually required).
Antibiotics made **surgery and chemotherapy safer** by controlling infection.
Death rates from **bacterial pneumonia, TB, sepsis and infected wounds** fell sharply after antibiotics were introduced.
Antibiotics only treat **bacterial** infections; they do not reduce the burden of viral diseases such as flu.
Overall **life expectancy** rose partly because of antibiotics, along with vaccination, sanitation and better nutrition.
Exam answers should say that antibiotics have **greatly reduced deaths from bacterial disease** (spec wording).
core.h: Impact: reduced deaths from bacterial disease
core.p: Before antibiotics became widely available in the 1940s, a scratch, a throat infection or childbirth could lead to **fatal blood poisoning**, and diseases such as **pneumonia, tuberculosis and sepsis** killed huge numbers of people. Penicillin was discovered by **Alexander Fleming** in 1928 and developed into a usable drug by **Florey and Chain** during the Second World War. Antibiotics **greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases** and made modern surgery, cancer treatment and organ transplants much safer, because patients can be protected from bacterial infection. This is why the spread of resistance is such a threat: we could lose these gains.

bullets: Viruses are **not made of cells**: no cell wall, cytoplasm or ribosomes of their own.
Viruses **reproduce inside living cells** and use the host cell's machinery.
Antibiotics target **bacterial** features (e.g. cell wall), which viruses do not have.
**It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues** (spec wording), because the virus hides inside our cells.
Taking antibiotics for a **cold or flu** (both viral) is **useless** and encourages resistance.
Viral diseases are controlled mainly by **vaccination** and by treating symptoms; a few have specific **antiviral drugs**.
Examples of viral diseases: **measles, HIV, flu, common cold, chickenpox**; examples of bacterial diseases: **salmonella food poisoning, gonorrhoea, tuberculosis, strep throat**.
core.p: **Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.** A virus is not a cell: it is a tiny particle made of **genetic material inside a protein coat**. It has no cell wall of its own, no ribosomes and no metabolism. It **reproduces by entering a host cell** and using the host cell's own machinery to make new virus particles. Antibiotics target structures and processes found **in bacteria**, so there is nothing for them to attack in a virus. A drug that attacks a virus inside a body cell would be much more likely to **damage the body's own cells** too, which is why developing safe antiviral drugs is difficult. Some antiviral drugs do exist, but they target specific stages of a particular virus.

bullets: **Step 1:** random **mutation** gives some bacteria a resistance gene (this happens by chance, not because the antibiotic is present).
**Step 2:** the antibiotic **kills non-resistant bacteria**.
**Step 3:** the resistant bacteria **survive** and **reproduce** (as fast as every 20 minutes), passing on the gene.
**Step 4:** the resistant strain **spreads** through the population, so the infection can no longer be treated with that antibiotic.
Resistance genes can be passed between bacteria on **plasmids**, even between species.
The antibiotic does **not** cause the mutation; it only **selects** for bacteria that already have it.
Bacteria do not 'get used to' the drug; **individuals do not change**, the **population** changes.
Higher tier idea: the rate of evolution is fast because of **short generation time** and **huge numbers**.
core.h: Antibiotic resistance: how it arises (natural selection)
core.p: Bacteria reproduce very quickly by binary fission, and **mutations** (random changes in their DNA) happen from time to time. Occasionally a mutation gives a bacterium **resistance** to an antibiotic, for example by changing the target site so the drug no longer fits. When the population is treated with the antibiotic, **non-resistant bacteria are killed**, but the **resistant bacteria survive**, face less competition and **reproduce**, passing the resistance gene to their offspring (vertical transfer) and sometimes to other bacteria on plasmids. Over time the **resistant strain becomes more common**, so the antibiotic no longer works. This is **natural selection**, and the antibiotic is the **selection pressure**.

bullets: **MRSA** = methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*; resistant to many commonly used antibiotics.
Spreads in **hospitals** by contact; important control measures are **hand washing**, **isolating infected patients** and **cleaning**.
Resistant strains are a major **public health threat**: infections take longer to treat and cause more deaths.
**Multidrug-resistant TB** needs long courses of several drugs and is hard to cure.
The World Health Organization treats antibiotic resistance as a **global health emergency**.
If resistance continues to spread, routine surgery and cancer treatment could become **riskier again**.
Always name **MRSA** when asked for an example of a resistant strain.
core.p: **MRSA** (methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*) is the standard example in the spec of a bacterium that has become resistant to several antibiotics. It can cause serious infections, particularly in **hospitals**, where patients with weakened immune systems and open wounds are exposed and antibiotics are used heavily. Other concerns include drug-resistant forms of **tuberculosis** and **gonorrhoea**. When no effective antibiotic is left, infections that were once easily treated can become life-threatening again.

bullets: **Do not overuse or misuse antibiotics:** e.g. not for viral infections such as colds and flu.
**Complete the course:** stopping when you feel better leaves some bacteria alive that can multiply and may be resistant.
**Restrict agricultural use:** avoid routine antibiotics for healthy animals.
**Hygiene in hospitals:** hand washing, screening, isolation reduce the spread of resistant strains such as MRSA.
**Develop new antibiotics**, but the development is slow and the rate of discovery is **lower than the rate at which resistance appears**.
**Use the right antibiotic** (narrow spectrum) identified by testing.
**Vaccination** reduces infections and therefore antibiotic use.
Public information campaigns (**'antibiotics are not for colds'**) help change expectations.
core.p: Because resistance comes from natural selection, the way to slow it is to **reduce selection pressure and the spread of resistant bacteria**. Doctors should **not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately**, for example for **viral infections** or minor infections that the body will clear alone. Patients should **complete the full course** so that all the bacteria are killed, including those that are slightly less sensitive; stopping early leaves survivors that can multiply. Farmers should avoid routine use of antibiotics in healthy livestock. Hospitals should follow strict **hygiene** to stop spread. Finally, **new antibiotics** need to be developed, but this is **slow and expensive**, and the number of new antibiotics is low.

bullets: **Painkillers** (analgesics) reduce **pain**; some also lower **fever**.
They treat **symptoms**, **not the cause**; the pathogen is still present.
They **do not kill bacteria or viruses**.
Examples: **paracetamol**, **ibuprofen**, **aspirin** (aspirin should not be given to young children).
Other symptom-relief medicines: **antihistamines**, **decongestants**, **cough syrups**.
Painkillers can be **harmful in overdose** (paracetamol damages the liver), so dosage instructions must be followed.
A person with a bacterial infection needs **antibiotics** as well as, not instead of, any painkiller.
Drug testing links: all medicines must pass **trials** for safety and effectiveness (see drug development).
core.h: Painkillers and other medicines: treating symptoms
core.p: **Painkillers** such as **paracetamol, aspirin and ibuprofen** relieve pain and, in some cases, reduce fever and inflammation. They treat the **symptoms** of a disease, not the **cause**. They **do not kill pathogens** and so they **do not cure** an infection. Other medicines used to relieve symptoms include **decongestants, cough medicines, antihistamines and anti-diarrhoea drugs**. Using painkillers can make a person feel better, but the immune system (and, for bacterial infections, antibiotics) still has to deal with the pathogen. Painkillers and antibiotics should not be confused in exam answers.

bullets: **Vaccine:** prevents; contains antigens; creates **memory cells**; works for **viruses and bacteria**.
**Antibiotic:** treats; kills **bacteria only**; works while the drug is present; **resistance** can develop.
**Painkiller:** relieves; treats **symptoms**; does **not kill pathogens**; no resistance issue.
**Antiviral:** treats some **viral** infections by blocking virus-specific steps; not covered in detail.
When should each be used? Vaccine **before** infection; antibiotic **during bacterial** infection; painkiller **any time** for symptom relief.
None of these gives a **cure for all diseases**: non-communicable diseases need different treatment.
Link to **drug development**: new medicines go through preclinical and clinical trials before use.
core.p: Exam questions often test whether you know the **different purposes** of these three. A **vaccine** prevents disease by stimulating the immune system. An **antibiotic** treats a bacterial disease by killing the bacteria. A **painkiller** treats the symptoms of any disease but does not remove the pathogen. A clear comparison also helps with 'suggest which treatment' questions. For a bacterial infection with pain and fever, the best treatment is an **antibiotic** (to cure) plus a **painkiller** (for comfort). For a viral infection, antibiotics are useless, so you can treat symptoms and rely on the immune system, and use vaccines to prevent future cases.

bullets: Spread the **bacteria evenly** over **sterile agar**, place **discs** with forceps, **tape the lid**, **incubate at 25 degrees C**.
Measure the **diameter** of each clear zone; **radius = diameter / 2**; **area = pi x r squared**.
**Larger zone = more effective** antibiotic against that bacterium.
**No zone** = resistant, or the antibiotic is not effective against these bacteria.
**Colonies growing inside a zone** show some individuals are resistant.
Use a **control disc** and keep **variables** constant: same bacteria, agar depth, disc size and incubation time.
Aseptic technique and safety rules apply: never open the plate after incubation; sterilise before disposal.
**Results show susceptibility**, not whether the drug is safe in humans; that needs clinical trials.
core.h: Testing antibiotics in the lab (link to the required practical)
core.p: In the lab, the effectiveness of antibiotics is tested by growing a **lawn of bacteria** on agar and placing **discs soaked in antibiotics** on it. After incubation at about **25 degrees C** in school, a **clear zone of inhibition** appears around a disc where the bacteria could not grow. A **larger zone** means the bacteria are more susceptible to that antibiotic. **No zone** means the bacteria are **resistant** to it. A **control disc** (sterile water) shows that the paper alone does not stop growth. The area of the zone is calculated from the diameter using **area = pi x r squared**. This is a **Biology-only** practical in the cell biology topic, but it links to this topic.

bullets: **Divisions** = total time / division time (same units).
**Population** = starting number x 2^n.
**Percentage resistant** = resistant / total x 100.
**Trend description:** say whether resistance is increasing, by how much, and quote data from the axes.
**Link cause and effect:** more antibiotic use gives more selection pressure, so a higher proportion of resistant bacteria.
**Evaluating data:** correlation does not prove causation; look for other variables.
**Area of clear zone** = pi x r squared (radius is half the diameter).
core.h: Maths skills: growth of resistant bacteria and data analysis
core.p: Questions on this topic regularly include calculations. If a resistant bacterium divides every 20 or 30 minutes, the population doubles each time, so the number after n divisions is the starting number x 2 to the power n. You may need to find the number of divisions from the time, work with percentages of resistant bacteria and express large numbers in **standard form**. You may also be given data on the **number of resistant cases over time** and asked to describe the trend or suggest causes. Always show your working and quote figures with units.

bullets: Link: **bacterial structure** (cell wall, plasmids) and **binary fission**.
Link: **mutation, variation and natural selection** (evolution topic).
Link: **vaccination** and **herd immunity** reduce the need for antibiotics.
Link: **drug testing** (preclinical and clinical trials, placebo, double-blind).
Link: **ethics:** use of antibiotics in farming; global access to medicine.
In a 6-mark answer include: what antibiotics do, why they do not work on viruses, how resistance arises, how to reduce it, and a conclusion.
Never say 'the antibiotic makes bacteria resistant' or 'bacteria adapt'; say 'random mutation' and 'natural selection'.
core.h: Links to other topics and how to write top-mark answers
core.p: Antibiotics and painkillers connect to several other topics. **Cell structure** explains why antibiotics target bacteria and not human cells; **evolution by natural selection** explains resistance; **vaccination** is the preventative alternative; **drug development** describes how new antibiotics are tested; and **ethics and society** include arguments about overuse in agriculture and the need for funding new drugs. In extended answers write in a logical chain (cause, effect, consequence) and use key terms precisely: **bacteria, viruses, antibiotic, resistant, mutation, selection pressure, reproduce, symptoms, pathogen**.

exam: **State what an antibiotic is (1 to 2 marks):** a medicine such as penicillin that cures bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.

**Explain why antibiotics do not work against viruses (2 marks):** viruses live and reproduce inside body cells (1); it is difficult to kill them without damaging body tissue / antibiotics target bacteria (1).

**Explain how resistance develops (4 marks):** random mutation gives some bacteria resistance (1); antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria (1); resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (1); resistant strain spreads / population now mostly resistant (1).
**Reducing resistance (2 to 3 marks):** do not overuse antibiotics or use them for viral infections (1); complete the full course (1); develop new antibiotics / hygiene to stop spread (1).
**What is the purpose of a painkiller? (1 to 2 marks):** relieves pain/symptoms (1) but does not kill the pathogen (1).
**Practical data (3 to 4 marks):** larger zone of inhibition = more effective; compare areas using pi x r squared; no zone = resistant; use of control disc.
**Calculations:** divisions = time / division time; population = start x 2^n; show every step and give standard form when asked.
**Use the right terms:** 'mutation', 'selection', 'resistant strain', 'reproduce'; avoid 'adapt', 'build up immunity', 'germs'.
**Compare antibiotics, vaccines and painkillers** with the three purposes: cure bacterial infection, prevent disease, relieve symptoms.
**Evaluate (6 marks):** benefits of antibiotics (reduced deaths, safer surgery) against drawbacks (resistance, side effects, overuse); give an example (MRSA) and a justified conclusion.
**Command words:** 'state' = short fact; 'explain' = reasons with because; 'suggest' = apply to a new situation; 'evaluate' = weigh up and conclude.

mistakes.r: Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens; they only kill bacteria. Colds and flu are caused by viruses.
mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill viruses / treat colds and flu.

mistakes.r: Resistance arises by random mutation; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria and the resistant ones survive and reproduce (natural selection).
mistakes.w: Bacteria become resistant because they get used to the antibiotic.

mistakes.r: It is the bacteria that become resistant to the antibiotic, not people.
mistakes.w: People or the body become resistant to antibiotics.

mistakes.r: Painkillers only treat the symptoms (pain); they do not kill pathogens.
mistakes.w: Painkillers kill the pathogen / cure the disease.

mistakes.r: Specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics.
mistakes.w: Any antibiotic will work on any bacterial infection.

mistakes.r: Using antibiotics unnecessarily increases selection pressure and the spread of resistant strains; they should only be used for bacterial infections.
mistakes.w: Antibiotics are needed to fight all infections, including viral ones, to be safe.

mistakes.r: The mutation occurs by chance before treatment; the antibiotic only selects for bacteria that already have it.
mistakes.w: The antibiotic causes the mutation that makes bacteria resistant.

mistakes.r: Complete the full course so that all the bacteria are killed and none are left to multiply and possibly become resistant.
mistakes.w: Stop taking the antibiotic once you feel better.

mistakes.r: Antibiotics target features of bacteria (e.g. cell wall) so they do not harm human cells; side effects are different (e.g. killing gut bacteria).
mistakes.w: Antibiotics also kill our own cells, which is why they have side effects.

summary: AQA 4.3.1.8: you must know that antibiotics such as penicillin cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body, that specific bacteria need specific antibiotics, that they have greatly reduced deaths but resistant strains are a concern, that antibiotics cannot kill viruses (which are hard to target without damaging body tissue), and that painkillers treat symptoms without killing pathogens. It is the base for resistance, natural selection and drug development questions.

terms.d: A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.
An antibiotic that kills bacteria by preventing the formation of the bacterial cell wall.
Single-celled prokaryotic organisms, some of which are pathogens; they can be killed by antibiotics.
A non-cellular pathogen that reproduces inside host cells; it cannot be killed by antibiotics.
The ability of bacteria to survive antibiotic treatment because of a genetic mutation, so that the antibiotic no longer kills them.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; a bacterium resistant to several antibiotics and a serious problem in hospitals.
A random change in the genetic material of an organism, which can give bacteria resistance to an antibiotic.
The process by which individuals with characteristics best suited to their environment survive and reproduce, passing on their genes.
An environmental factor (such as an antibiotic) that makes some individuals more likely to survive than others.
A medicine (for example paracetamol) that relieves pain or other symptoms but does not kill pathogens.
A feature of a disease that a patient experiences, such as pain, fever or a cough.
Simple cell division in bacteria in which one cell splits into two identical cells, as often as once every 20 minutes.
The clear area around an antibiotic disc on an agar plate where bacteria have not grown.
Working on one particular type only; specific bacteria need specific antibiotics.
A small ring of DNA in bacteria that can carry resistance genes and be passed between bacteria.
Introducing dead or inactive pathogens into the body so that white blood cells produce antibodies and memory cells, preventing future infection.

worked.ans: Model answer: A random mutation gives some bacteria resistance to an antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance gene. Over time the resistant strain becomes more common and spreads to other people, so the antibiotic is no longer effective.
worked.q: Explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA arise and spread. (4 marks)
steps: Mutation: a random mutation in a bacterium's DNA makes it resistant to an antibiotic.
Selection: when the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but resistant bacteria survive.
Reproduction: the survivors reproduce (binary fission) and pass the resistance gene on.
Spread: the resistant strain becomes common, so the antibiotic no longer works and the strain spreads between people.

worked.ans: 40 960 bacteria = 4.1 x 10^4 (2 s.f.). All of these are resistant, so antibiotic X will no longer work.
worked.q: A patient has 10 000 bacteria. One in every 1000 is resistant to antibiotic X. Antibiotic X kills all non-resistant bacteria. The resistant bacteria divide every 30 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 6 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (4 marks)

worked.ans: A = 113 mm^2 and B = 314 mm^2 (3 s.f.). Antibiotic B is the most effective because it has the largest zone of inhibition; the bacteria are resistant to C.
worked.q: Discs of antibiotics A and B were placed on a lawn of bacteria. The clear zone around A had a diameter of 12 mm and around B 20 mm; disc C had no zone. Calculate the area of each zone and say which antibiotic is most effective. (5 marks)
steps: A: radius = 12 / 2 = 6 mm; area = pi x 6^2 = pi x 36 = 113 mm^2.
B: radius = 20 / 2 = 10 mm; area = pi x 10^2 = 314 mm^2.
B's zone area is 314 / 113 = 2.8 times bigger than A's.
C: no zone, so the bacteria are resistant to antibiotic C (or it has no effect).
